295.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (1 of 7)
295.hook: the most famous book about yoga opens with one word, and the word is now
295.tomorrow: Patanjali 1.2: the stilling of the mind's turnings (2 of 7)
295.howItsDone: The Yoga Sutras are studied line by line with a teacher and a commentary, often chanted in Sanskrit first; many yoga schools, in India and around the world, open their study with the first sutra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shatpadi, the hymn that closed Dvaita and beyond: the wave belongs to the ocean, never the ocean to the wave. Two, and the space between is love. Today, a new week, and a new book.
screen: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: January, and the gym is packed. Monday, and the diet starts. The meditation app can wait until work calms down. A better time is always coming, and it's never quite this one. Then there's a short Sanskrit book about yoga that isn't about the poses. It's about the mind. You might expect it to open with a warning, or a promise, or a long list of what you need first. It opens with one word. And the word is now.
screen: `MONDAY. JANUARY. WHEN THINGS CALM DOWN.` → `A SHORT BOOK ABOUT THE MIND.` → `ITS FIRST WORD: NOW.`

segments.voice: The book is the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. A sutra is a thread: a short line, packed tight, meant to be memorized and then unpacked by a teacher. The book strings them into four chapters. Who was Patanjali? Honestly, nobody knows much. Scholars' guesses for its date span several centuries. Tradition tells stories about him, including that he was an incarnation of the great serpent who holds up the world. The first thread, in Sanskrit, is atha yoga anushasanam. Now, the teaching of yoga. Atha, now, is a word Sanskrit books often start with. The Brahma Sutras open the same way: now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. Traditionally the word is also considered auspicious, a good sound to begin with. The classic commentary, traditionally credited to Vyasa, says atha marks a beginning: here the teaching starts. Later teachers found more in it. Now means the preparation is over. Now means you've arrived with whatever brought you here: a restless mind, a bad week, curiosity. Now means yoga isn't something that happens after your life gets sorted out. It's the sorting. This week walks the first sixteen threads, slowly. Tomorrow, the definition of what yoga actually is. Today, just the first word.
screen: `A SUTRA IS A THREAD.` · `WHO WAS PATANJALI? NOBODY KNOWS MUCH.` · `ATHA: NOW, THE TEACHING BEGINS.` · `YOGA ISN'T AFTER YOUR LIFE. IT'S THE SORTING.` · then, large: `ATHA YOGĀNUŚĀSANAM.`

segments.voice: Sit exactly as you are, without fixing your posture or waiting for quiet, and notice what's here: the nearest sound, the feeling in your hands, the mood you brought in. Whenever your mind leaves for later or earlier, say the word gently, now, and come back; you'll probably say it many times, and every time counts as starting. If you pray, you can offer this now to God.
Atha, now. The first thread of the Yoga Sutras is atha yoga anushasanam: now, the teaching of yoga. Everything the book will teach, it teaches to someone who has already begun.
Your line: now. Not Monday, not January, not later. Day two ninety-five, and you've already begun.

296.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (2 of 7)
296.hook: the whole definition of yoga, in four Sanskrit words, and not one of them is about stretching
296.tomorrow: Patanjali 1.3–1.4: the seer rests in itself (3 of 7)
296.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras often memorize 1.2 in Sanskrit, and many yoga teachers in India and abroad quote it as the definition of yoga before teaching any posture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali 1.1: atha, now. The book of yoga begins with someone who has already begun.

Say the word yoga and what comes up is stretching: a class at the gym, a mat, a pose with a funny name. Fair enough. That's what the word means on a lot of streets. Now open the Yoga Sutras to the second line, where Patanjali actually defines the word. Four Sanskrit words. Not one is about the body: no breath, no posture, no flexibility. They're about something you carry everywhere, something that's been running since you woke up this morning, and is running right now, as you listen.
screen: `STRETCHING. A MAT. A POSE.` → `THE SECOND LINE.` → `FOUR WORDS, NONE ABOUT THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Here it is: yogash chitta vritti nirodhah. Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Chitta is the mind in the widest sense: thinking, feeling, remembering, the whole inner stuff. Vritti means a turning, a whirl, a movement, from a root that means to turn, like a wheel. Those are the thoughts, but also the moods, the memories, the half-conscious commentary: she didn't text back, I'm hungry, what was that song. Nirodha means stilling, restraining, bringing to rest. So for Patanjali, yoga is what happens when the whirling settles. Vivekananda, in his lectures on this book, used a lake. When the wind blows, ripples cover the surface and you can't see the bottom. When the water goes still, you can see all the way down. Notice what the definition doesn't say. It doesn't say yoga is emptying your head by force. Nirodha can be translated restraint or cessation, and teachers often hear it as a settling, like a pond going still, not a lid slammed down. And the ripples aren't bad. They're just ripples. Teachers often say the whole rest of the book unpacks this one short line: what the turnings are, why they won't settle, and how, slowly, they do. So when someone says they're bad at yoga because they can't touch their toes, Patanjali would have a gentle surprise for them.
screen: `YOGAŚ CITTA-VṚTTI-NIRODHAḤ.` · `CHITTA, VRITTI, NIRODHA: MIND, TURNING, STILL.` · `A LAKE WITH NO WIND.` · `STILLING, NOT SLAMMING A LID.` · then, large: `YOGA IS THE STILLING OF THE MIND'S TURNINGS.`

segments.voice: Picture a lake in the morning with a little wind on it: that's your mind right now. Don't try to stop the wind; breathe slowly and watch each ripple, a thought, a sound, a small worry, cross the surface and go, and when the water is flat for a moment between them, rest there. If you pray, you can let that stillness be your prayer.
Vritti, a turning of the mind. Yoga is the stilling of these turnings: chitta, vritti, nirodha. Mind, turning, stillness.
Your line: still now. The whirling can settle, ripple by ripple. That's day two ninety-six.

297.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (3 of 7)
297.hook: when the lake goes still, who is it that's looking?
297.howItsDone: In classical yoga study, sutras 1.3 and 1.4 are read with the Samkhya distinction between purusha, the seer, and prakriti, the seen, and meditation is described as learning to witness the mind rather than be swept along by it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vritti: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings. Chitta, vritti, nirodha, and the lake going still.

An email lands, or a comment, and you are furious. For twenty minutes you are the anger. There's no you and the anger, just anger wearing your face, typing the reply. Then something shifts. Maybe you take a walk, maybe you sleep on it, and suddenly you can see the anger, like weather passing over a field. It's there, but you're not it anymore. Something in you was watching the whole time. Patanjali's next two threads are about that something.
screen: `YOU ARE THE ANGER.` → `THEN YOU CAN SEE IT.` → `SOMETHING WAS WATCHING.`

segments.voice: Thread three: then the seer rests in its own nature. In Sanskrit, tada drashtuh svarupe avasthanam. Tada, then: when the turnings have stilled. Drashta, the seer, the one who sees. Svarupa, its own form, its own true shape. Thread four says what happens the rest of the time: vritti sarupyam itaratra. Otherwise, the seer takes on the form of the turnings. It looks exactly like its thoughts. The anger arrives, and you become angry. The worry arrives, and you become worried. Teachers in this tradition use a picture. Put a clear crystal next to a red flower, and the crystal looks red. It isn't red. It never was. It's just sitting next to something red. So who is the seer? Here Patanjali leans on a closely related Hindu philosophy called Samkhya, which divides everything in two: the seer, called purusha, pure awareness, and everything seen, called prakriti. That includes the body and, surprisingly, the mind itself. Thoughts are part of what's seen, not the one seeing. Your thoughts are scenery. Different schools of Hindu thought describe the seer differently; you met some of those debates in the last two weeks. But on this point they sound alike: you are not your weather.
screen: `TADĀ DRAṢṬUḤ SVARŪPE 'VASTHĀNAM.` · `OTHERWISE, IT LOOKS LIKE ITS THOUGHTS.` · `A CRYSTAL NEXT TO A RED FLOWER.` · `THOUGHTS ARE SEEN, NOT THE SEER.` · then, large: `YOU ARE NOT YOUR WEATHER.`

segments.voice: Let a thought come, any thought, and instead of following it, notice it the way you'd notice a car going by. Each time, step back half a step: there's the thought, and here is the one seeing it; you don't have to name the seer, just notice that noticing is happening, and that it isn't going anywhere. If you pray, you can rest in that quiet as a prayer.
Drashta, the seer, the one who sees. When the turnings still, the seer rests in its own nature. Otherwise it takes the shape of its thoughts.
Your line: now. A feeling can be here while you see it. Day two ninety-seven, done.

298.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (4 of 7)
298.hook: Patanjali sorts every thought you'll ever have into five kinds, and one of them is sleep
298.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras often learn the five vrittis as a list and use them in meditation, noting which kind of thought is arising rather than following it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, drashta, the seer: when the turnings still, it rests in itself; otherwise it looks like its thoughts, a crystal next to a red flower.

Try to count your thoughts from this morning. It can't be done: the coffee, the weather, a face from high school, an argument you haven't had yet. It feels like chaos. Patanjali looked at that same kind of chaos and did something very calm. He sorted it. Every turning of the mind, he says, fits one of five kinds. Five drawers for everything you'll ever think. And one of the drawers is labeled sleep.
screen: `TOO MANY THOUGHTS TO COUNT.` → `FIVE DRAWERS.` → `ONE IS LABELED SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Thread five: the turnings are five, and some bring pain and some don't. Thread six lists them. First, right knowing: seeing what's actually there, reasoning well from it, or trusting a reliable witness. Second, error: knowing something that isn't so, like the rope in the dusk you take for a snake, an example you know from Advaita. Third, a slippery one: imagination, or knowledge from words alone, ideas with no real object behind them. A stock example in Indian philosophy is the horn of a hare. You understand the phrase. There's no such thing. Fourth, sleep, and that's the surprise. Deep sleep, Patanjali says, is still a turning of the mind, one that rests on absence, on nothing. The proof, the commentators say, is that you wake up and remember: I slept well. Something was there to know it. Fifth, memory: holding on to what you've already experienced. Why does the list matter? Teachers say that once you can name a turning, it has less grip. It's not the truth arriving. It's a memory. It's an imagined scene. It's the rope again. And remember thread five: some turnings bring pain and some don't. Patanjali isn't asking you to hate your thoughts. Right knowing is a turning too, and a helpful one. The work of yoga is to know which drawer you're in, and in the end, to let all five go quiet.
screen: `PRAMĀṆA-VIPARYAYA-VIKALPA-NIDRĀ-SMṚTAYAḤ.` · `RIGHT KNOWING, ERROR, IMAGINATION.` · `SLEEP, AND MEMORY.` · `NAME THE TURNING; IT LOSES ITS GRIP.` · then, large: `FIVE DRAWERS FOR EVERY THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Let the mind do what it does, and when a thought comes, give it a drawer, softly: memory, imagination, knowing, error, or even sleep if you drift toward drowsiness. You don't need to be right about the drawer; label it, let it go, and notice the quiet between labels. If you pray, you can rest in that quiet.
Nidra, sleep, one of the five turnings of the mind. Right knowing, error, imagination, nidra and memory: five drawers for every thought.
Your line: now. A worry can be real knowing, or only imagination. See you tomorrow.

299.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (5 of 7)
299.hook: the whole method of yoga in two words, and Krishna said the same two words to Arjuna
299.tomorrow: Patanjali 1.13–1.14: practice, over a long time (6 of 7)
299.howItsDone: Hindu teachers of meditation often pair abhyasa and vairagya, citing both Yoga Sutra 1.12 and Bhagavad Gita 6.35, and describe daily practice as returning again and again without clinging to results.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nidra, sleep, one of the five turnings: right knowing, error, imagination, sleep and memory. Five drawers for every thought.

My mind is restless. Holding it still is like holding the wind. That's Arjuna in the Gita, more or less, a few months ago on this path, stopping Krishna somewhere in the sixth chapter. Anyone who has tried to meditate for five minutes knows the feeling. Krishna doesn't argue. He agrees: yes, the mind is hard to hold. Then he gives two words for how it's done. Patanjali, in thread twelve, gives the very same two.
screen: `ARJUNA: MY MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA AGREES.` → `TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Thread twelve: abhyasa vairagyabhyam tan nirodhah. By practice and non-attachment, they are stilled; they, meaning the turnings. Two words carry the whole method. Abhyasa, practice: coming back, again and again, to the thing you've chosen. Vairagya, non-attachment: letting go of the pull. Literally it means without coloring, without the red flower staining the crystal. Teachers often say the two are like the two wings of a bird. One wing alone, and you fly in circles. Practice without letting go becomes grinding: you sit every day, jaw clenched, demanding results. Letting go without practice becomes drifting: you're very relaxed and nothing changes. Coming back, and not clutching. And here is the Gita's answer to Arjuna, in that sixth chapter: the mind is restless, hard to hold, but it can be held by practice and by dispassion. The same pair, in the same order. Two great texts, from different schools, agree on the method. Now make it small. Practice is the phone you put face down again. Non-attachment is not caring, for a moment, whether it buzzes. Practice is returning to the breath. Non-attachment is not needing the breath to feel special. Tomorrow and the day after, Patanjali takes each wing on its own.
screen: `ABHYĀSA-VAIRĀGYĀBHYĀṀ TAN-NIRODHAḤ.` · `ABHYASA: COMING BACK, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `VAIRAGYA: LETTING GO OF THE PULL.` · `TWO WINGS OF ONE BIRD.` · then, large: `PRACTICE, AND LET GO.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing to return to: the breath at the nose, a word, or the sound of the room. When the mind wanders, and it will, come back without scolding it, no clutching, no scorekeeping: come back, let go, the whole method in small. If you pray, the thing you return to can be a name of God.
Abhyasa vairagya, practice and non-attachment, the turnings are stilled. Two wings: one alone, you fly in circles.
Your line: now. One wing comes back; the other lets go. One more day to three hundred.

300.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (6 of 7)
300.hook: day three hundred, and Patanjali's three conditions for a practice that holds
300.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often cite 1.14 to explain why daily practice matters more than intensity: a practice kept over a long time, steadily and with respect, becomes firmly grounded.

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhyasa vairagya: practice and non-attachment, two wings of one bird. Today, the first wing up close.

Three hundred days. However you got here, day after day or in fits and starts, it's a fair place to ask a plain question. Some sittings feel like something. Some feel like nothing at all, like brushing your teeth. So what makes a practice actually hold, not through a week of enthusiasm, but for years? Patanjali answers in a single line, with three conditions, and none of them is feeling good while you do it.
screen: `THREE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `SOME DAYS, NOTHING AT ALL.` → `WHAT MAKES A PRACTICE HOLD?`

segments.voice: First, thread thirteen defines practice. Abhyasa is the effort to stay there: to remain steady in that stillness. Not the stillness itself, notice. The effort. The returning. So every time you drift and come back, that isn't failure. That's the practice happening. Then thread fourteen: it becomes firmly grounded when it's attended to for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion. A long time: dirgha kala. Not a weekend retreat. Seasons. Years. Without break: nairantarya. The commentators mean steadiness, a thread that keeps running. Some teachers read it kindly: not perfection, but a practice that doesn't wait for ideal conditions. With devotion: satkara, doing something with respect, with care, as if it matters. The same practice done carelessly and done with care are not the same practice. And the result? Dridha bhumi. Firm ground, like soil walked on so many times it becomes a path you can stand on in a storm. Look at what the line leaves out. Patanjali doesn't say you'll feel peaceful every day. He doesn't promise fireworks. He promises ground. Three hundred days is a real start on the first condition.
screen: `PRACTICE IS THE EFFORT TO RETURN.` · `A LONG TIME, WITHOUT BREAK.` · `AND WITH DEVOTION: SATKARA.` · `THE RESULT: FIRM GROUND.` · then, large: `SA TU DĪRGHA-KĀLA-NAIRANTARYA-SATKĀRĀSEVITO DṚḌHA-BHŪMIḤ.`

segments.voice: Treat these minutes with a little extra care: straighten your back as if someone you respect were in the room, and breathe in and out slowly, all the way. When you drift, come back, and count the coming back as the practice, not the drifting as a failure; nothing needs to happen, you're laying ground. If you pray, you can offer these three hundred days to God, the ordinary ones most of all.
Abhyasa, practice, the effort to return. It becomes firm ground over a long time, steadily, with care.
Your line: now. Even an ordinary thing, done with satkara, is practice. Three hundred days, and counting.

301.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (7 of 7)
301.hook: letting go of what you've seen, and of what you've only heard about, and then a letting go beyond that
301.tomorrow: the lineage tracks begin: karma, bhakti, jnana
301.howItsDone: In Hindu teaching, vairagya is not only for monks: householders are taught to hold wealth, family and even religious rewards loosely, and the Yoga Sutras' opening chapter is often studied as a complete short course in meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhyasa: a long time, without break, with care, until it becomes firm ground. Today, the other wing, and the week closes.

The last slice of cake. The ping of a new message. The feeling of being right in an argument. Some things pull at you because you've tasted them. Others pull because you've only heard about them: the trip everyone posts about, the life your cousin seems to have, the perfect calm that serious meditators supposedly reach. Patanjali noticed both kinds of pull and named them in the same breath. Then, in the very next thread, he went one step further.
screen: `WHAT YOU'VE TASTED.` → `WHAT YOU'VE ONLY HEARD ABOUT.` → `ONE STEP FURTHER.`

segments.voice: Thread fifteen: non-attachment is the mastery of one who no longer thirsts for things seen, or things heard about. Seen means this world: the cake, the praise, the paycheck. Heard about means everything promised by tradition or rumor, and the old commentators include heavenly rewards here too. Even spiritual prizes can become one more thing to crave. Patanjali's word for the result is vashikara: mastery, being in charge of the pull rather than pulled by it. He doesn't say the cake disappears. You can still eat the cake. It just doesn't own you. Then thread sixteen, the higher kind: from knowing the seer, the purusha, comes freedom from thirst even for the gunas, the basic strands that make up everything in nature. That's letting go at the root: not of this craving or that one, but of the whole weave, because you've seen what you are underneath it. Now look back at the week. Thread one: now. Two: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings. Three and four: the seer resting in itself, or looking like its thoughts, a crystal beside a red flower. Five to eleven: the five turnings, sleep among them. Twelve: two wings, practice and letting go. Thirteen and fourteen: the long, steady, careful practice that becomes firm ground. And fifteen and sixteen: letting go of what you've tasted and what you've heard of, and at last, of the thirst itself. Sixteen threads, one week, and it all started with one word: now.
screen: `NO THIRST FOR THINGS SEEN OR HEARD OF.` · `VASHIKARA: MASTERY OF THE PULL.` · `THE HIGHER KIND: FREE AT THE ROOT.` · `SIXTEEN THREADS, ONE WEEK.` · then, large: `TAT PARAṀ PURUṢA-KHYĀTER GUṆA-VAITṚṢṆYAM.`

segments.voice: Let one pull come to mind, something you've tasted and want again, or something you've only heard about and want anyway, and notice where you feel it: the chest, the stomach, the hands. Breathe into that place and loosen your grip by one finger, then another; you don't have to give the thing up, only notice that the wanting doesn't have to own you. If you pray, you can offer the wanting to God.
Vairagya, non-attachment, mastery of the pull from what you've tasted and what you've heard of. All sixteen threads come down to this, all the way to the root.
Your line: now. The cake can stay; it just doesn't own you. That's the week, and day three hundred one.
